migrationNotes: Spine: one tool, Leibniz's law, is tried on a comic-book case, then on Descartes' proof that he is not his body, then on the objection that follows from that proof, and the lesson ends at the views that drop the proof's conclusion.

lesson.title: Mind and body

lead.text: In the comics, Clark Kent and Superman are one man with two names, though Lois Lane does not know it. She works beside the mild reporter every day and admires the hero who flies past her window. Because there is only one man, anything true of Superman is true of Clark Kent. If Superman can fly, so can Clark Kent.

That is a general rule about identity, known as Leibniz's law after the seventeenth-century philosopher Gottfried Leibniz: if A and B are the same thing, then whatever is true of A is true of B. The rule runs in one direction only. It says what must follow from being one thing, and it does not say the reverse.

The rule is most useful for showing that two things are different. If you can find a property that A has and B lacks, then A and B cannot be one thing. A house with a red door cannot be the same house as one without a red door. Descartes uses the rule in exactly this way when he argues that he is not his own body.
Apply the rule to the two names.

In the Meditations Descartes doubted everything he could, and he noticed an asymmetry. He could doubt that his body exists, since a demon or a dream might have invented it. He could not doubt that he himself exists, since doubting is a kind of thinking and something has to be doing the thinking.

He turned this into an argument. His body is something he can doubt exists, and he is not something he can doubt exists. By Leibniz's law, if he were his body then whatever is true of one would be true of the other, so he is not his body. He concluded that a person is a mind, a thinking thing with no size or place, joined to a body that has both. The view that mind and body are two different kinds of thing is called substance dualism, where a substance is something that exists in its own right.

steps.headline: Descartes: I can doubt that my body exists, but I cannot doubt that I exist. So I am not my body. Does it work?

workedSteps.text: Premise 1: my body has the property of being doubted by me. Premise 2: I lack that property, since I cannot doubt that I exist.
Leibniz's law: if I were my body, whatever is true of one would be true of the other.
So I am not my body. This stands only if “being doubted by me” is a real property, which the masked man puts in question.

lead.text: If a person is a mind joined to a body, the two must affect each other. A pinprick in a finger produces a feeling of pain, and a decision to raise your arm produces a raised arm. In 1643 Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia wrote to Descartes to ask how this could work.

Descartes held that bodies are extended, which means they take up space, while minds are not. A billiard ball moves another by touching it and pushing. Elisabeth asked how something with no size or place could touch anything, let alone push a body. If it cannot touch, it seems it cannot move. This objection, how two substances with nothing in common could act on each other, is called the interaction problem.

Descartes replied that we all know from experience that the mind moves the body. He compared the mind's action to heaviness, which pulls a stone down without any contact we can feel. Elisabeth was not persuaded, and she pressed him in further letters. Dualists have been looking for a better answer ever since.
Ask what kind of problem arises when two substances are supposed to act on each other.

Elisabeth's challenge can be written as an argument and tested as the sceptic's was in the last lesson. Let p stand for “the mind moves the body”, q for “the mind touches the body” and r for “the mind is extended”. Her first premise says that if the mind moves the body, it touches it. Her second says that if the mind touches the body, it is extended. Descartes accepts the third, that the mind is not extended.

In symbols the premises are p → q, q → r and ¬r, and the conclusion is ¬p, that the mind does not move the body. With three letters there are eight rows. To test the argument, start from ¬r, which is true only in the rows where r is false, and then see which of those rows keep the other two premises true. The practice question asks how many do.

The result matters for a dualist. If the argument is valid, then anyone who wants to keep the interaction has to deny one of its premises. One choice is to deny the first, that moving something requires touching it. That leaves the dualist to explain a kind of causing that needs no contact.

lead.text: A different response to the interaction problem is to deny that there are two substances. Physicalism holds that everything, minds included, is physical. One argument for it concerns causes. Every physical event that has a cause already has a sufficient physical cause, so if mental events also caused physical ones, each of those events would have two causes. That looks like an odd coincidence, and the simpler view is that the mental events doing the causing are themselves physical.

Physicalists then differ about how a mental state is physical. One view says that each type of mental state just is a type of brain state, in the way that lightning just is electrical discharge. Pain would be a pattern of nerve cells firing and nothing over and above it. This is the identity theory.

A weaker position keeps one physical substance but not a physical account of the mind. Property dualism says there is only one kind of substance, the physical, while mental properties such as the feel of pain are not physical properties. A brain would have both kinds. This avoids two substances, though it still owes an account of how a mental property makes a difference in the physical world.

premises.text: Every physical event that has a cause has a sufficient physical cause.
Some mental events cause physical events.
Those physical events are not caused twice over.

conclusion.text: Those mental events are physical events.

premises.text: If the mind moves the body, it touches the body.

The mind is not extended.

lead.text: In the 1950s U. T. Place and J. J. C. Smart proposed that a sensation such as pain is nothing over and above a process in the brain, as lightning is nothing over and above an electrical discharge.

reveal.text: That is the identity theory, proposed by Place and Smart in the 1950s. A weaker view, property dualism, keeps one physical substance but says mental properties are not physical properties.

lesson.orientation: Assess Descartes' case for dualism, Elisabeth's interaction problem and the physicalist alternatives.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The last lesson counted evidence as if someone were there to be moved by it. This lesson asks what that someone is. When you picture yourself thinking, you might picture a brain at work, or you might picture something that could never be weighed or photographed, a mind that merely uses the brain. People have argued for both answers for a very long time, and Descartes' answer, that the mind is a separate thing from the body, is still where the debate starts.

His case rests on an argument about what he could doubt, and judging it takes a logical tool that is easiest to meet in a comic book. We start with that tool, use it to test his argument, and then follow the objection that a princess put to him in 1643, which has never been answered to everyone's satisfaction.
The lesson closes with the views that say there is nothing here beyond the physical world.

intro.promise: By the end you'll test Descartes' argument for dualism with Leibniz's law, state Elisabeth's objection and name the main physicalist views.

recap.keyIdea: Leibniz's law can prove two things distinct, but only for real properties. Descartes' doubt argument is shaky for that reason, and Elisabeth's valid argument leaves dualists a premise to deny.

blocks.text: You found that the masked-man argument fails and set Descartes' doubt argument beside it. Elisabeth's question then became an argument, which you checked row by row before meeting the physicalist answers.

recap.nextHook: Some physicalists say a mind is defined by what it does and not by what it is made of. The next lesson asks whether that would let a machine have a mind.

questions.prompt: 'Lois believes Superman can fly. Lois does not believe Clark Kent can fly. So Superman is not Clark Kent.' The premises are true in the story and the conclusion is false. Is the argument valid or invalid?
hints: Recall the definition: can the premises be true while the conclusion is false?
The story itself supplies the situation you need.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Invalid: true premises with a false conclusion is exactly a counterexample. 'Being believed by Lois to fly' is not a property that Leibniz's law carries across.

questions.onCorrect: Invalid: both premises are true in the story and the conclusion is false.

misconceptions.feedback: The story itself supplies the situation: Superman is Clark Kent. Can both premises be true while the conclusion is false?

questions.prompt: Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia asked Descartes how an unextended mind could move an extended body. What is this objection to substance dualism called? Answer in one or two words.
hints: The problem concerns causation running between mind and body.
Its name describes the two substances acting on each other.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The interaction problem: how two substances with nothing in common could causally affect each other.

questions.onCorrect: The interaction problem: how substances with nothing in common could causally affect each other.

misconceptions.feedback: That names a different issue. Elisabeth asked how two such different substances could act on each other.

questions.prompt: Elisabeth's argument as 'p → q, q → r, ¬r, so ¬p' has eight truth-table rows. In how many are all three premises true?
hints: Start with ¬r: keep only rows where r is false.
Among those, q → r needs q to be false.
Then check p → q with q false.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ¬r leaves the rows with r false; q → r then needs q false; p → q then needs p false. One row remains, and ¬p is true in it.

questions.onCorrect: One row keeps all three premises true, and ¬p holds in it. The argument is valid.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many rows ¬r keeps. The other two premises remove more.
Check q → r where r is false: it needs q false. Then check p → q.

questions.prompt: U. T. Place and J. J. C. Smart held that each type of mental state, such as pain, is a type of brain state. Name their view.

questions.onCorrect: The identity theory: each type of mental state is a type of brain state.

questions.prompt: Which statement is Leibniz's law, the indiscernibility of identicals?
hints: The law goes from identity to properties, not the other way.

acceptedIdeas: If x is identical with y, then x and y share every property
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leibniz's law runs from identity to shared properties. The converse, from shared properties to identity, is the identity of indiscernibles.

choices.label: If x is identical with y, then x and y share every property

questions.onCorrect: Leibniz's law runs from identity to shared properties, never the other way.

questions.prompt: Name the view that there is only one kind of substance, physical, but that mental properties are not physical properties.

questions.onCorrect: Property dualism: one physical substance, with mental properties that are not physical ones.

questions.prompt: Does your friend's belief show that Sam and the mayor are different people? Answer yes or no.
hints: Her belief is about what she thinks, not about Sam.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. What she believes about the two names does not change who they pick out.

misconceptions.feedback: She has a view about one name and none about the other. Is that a fact about the man, or about her?
